title: Gold on the doubletrack
summary: A late-morning return to the Marlette Lake trail from Spooner Lake Trailhead, now that it's open again: Christian rode with Marley, Helena walked with Sofi, and the aspens were at full gold. About seven miles, with more time stopped for the trees than riding.

photos.caption: 10:47. A dog in a harness waits on the doubletrack between the aspens.
Helmet on, aspens on both sides, and the dog close behind.
11:01. Higher up: a sage meadow, gold aspens below the ridge.
11:19. Backlit aspen leaves against the shadowed trunks behind them.
One aspen, lit from behind, against the dark firs.
The same tree with the pines and a strip of blue sky above.
11:24. A selfie on the road, under the aspens.
A black dog and a big smile on the leaf-covered doubletrack.
11:51. The trail slips through a stand of orange aspens.
The trail to Marlette Lake by bike.
Marley and Me on the way up.

fieldNotes:
Is the brown dog in the harness Marley? If so, I'll name her in the post and episode.
Yes. Yes.

Who is the woman in the sun hat in photos 07 and 08? If it's Helena, I'll name her (Ha-Leen-Ah in the script). If it's someone else, is she OK appearing in the photos?
Yes and yes.

Whose is the black dog in photo 08, and did she ride or walk along with you, or did you meet on the trail?
Sofi and we are dog sitting for neighbors. Please do. Walked with Helena. Marley was with me and the bike.

Which trail or road was this (for example, North Canyon toward Marlette)? Should I name it?
Marlette Lake trail. From Spooner lake.

Did you ride alone and meet up later, or did everyone set out together from the trailhead?
Bit of both.

Anything that happened, a stop, a snack, or the tracker running long, that you'd like added? The notes were empty.
Snacks. Horses were on the trail. A lot more people than usual now that it’s open again. Ranger at gate said open all trails all days now. We had a note from before that was before it was closed for repairs.

I left out that Sofi belongs to neighbors, since it hints at home and at a house being empty; she's just "a black dog we were dog-sitting." OK?
Yes that’s good.

For "bit of both" I wrote that you rode and walked at your own speeds and met up again on the road. Is that right, or did you set out together and split later?
Set out together and split but met up again many times along the way. It was about and back trail not a loop.

The reopening is told as the ranger reported it (all trails open every day). OK to leave it as reported rather than checked?
Yes.

I added the general rule that bikes yield to horses on shared trails, without saying what you did. Keep it?
Of course. I always yield. In fact we were at a stream when the rode up and I could see the spot we were in was the best place for the horses to get to water so we packed up and left. We were ready to go and lucky to meet and see such beautiful creatures.

Where in the outing was the stream stop with the horses (on the way up, near the turnaround, or on the way back)? I placed it as "at one point" for now.
Back near start on way back.

At the stream, who was "we": you and Marley, or Helena and Sofi too? Was that also the snack stop?
Me and Marley only.

Were the horses being ridden (I wrote that they "rode up")? Any riders stay unnamed either way.
Yes. Friendly riders. And horses

Was the stream stop with Marley also where you had your snacks, or were the snacks with Helena and Sofi on the road?
Then back was a granola bar and I had it at the stream just before the horses rode up.

I moved the snacks to the stream (your granola bar) and took "There were snacks" out of the meet-up with Helena and Sofi on the road. Is that right, or did they have snacks on the road too?
We both had our own snacks.

post.title: Gold on the doubletrack
post.body:
I rolled out of Spooner Lake Trailhead a little after ten on a clear October morning, on the trail toward Marlette Lake. The last time I wrote up this trail was before it closed for repairs, so this was a return. The ranger at the gate said all the trails are open every day now, and it showed: a lot more people than usual, and horses on the trail too. On a shared trail, bikes yield to horses, and I always do. On the way back, near the start, Marley and I were stopped at a stream. I had a granola bar there, and just after, some friendly riders came up on their horses. I could see that the spot we were in was the best place for the horses to get to the water. We were ready to go anyway, so we packed up and left it to them. We were lucky to meet them and see such beautiful creatures.

It was a bit of both kind of outing. Marley came with me and the bike. Helena walked with Sofi, a black dog we were dog-sitting. We set out together, split up to go at our own speeds, and met up again many times along the way. We each carried our own snacks. It's an out-and-back trail, not a loop. The plan was simple: get up into the aspens while they were still at their peak and see how far the color went.

It went all the way. Within half an hour the doubletrack was a corridor of white trunks and yellow leaves, with a deep blue sky showing through the gaps at the top. Marley trotted ahead of me, then waited, then trotted ahead again. That became the rhythm of the morning.

Higher up the trail opened onto a meadow of sage, with a hillside of gold aspens below the ridgeline and a few dark firs standing in front of it. The aspens weren't all the same color. Some groves were pale lemon, some had gone orange, and a few still held some green.

Just after eleven I stopped riding and started photographing. The light was coming from behind the trees, so the leaves lit up while the pines behind them stayed in shadow. That contrast is what I was after: one gold aspen against a dark wall of conifers, framed tall so the tree fills the picture.

A few minutes later Helena and Sofi were with us on the road again: a big smile under a sun hat and a black dog who looked very pleased about everything.

The last stretch back down ran through a dense stand of aspens that had turned almost completely orange, with the trail slipping between them like a tunnel.

The numbers: about seven miles, a little over nine hundred feet of climbing, and a high point near 7,700 feet. I was moving for under an hour of a ride that took close to two. My top speed was about 22 miles an hour, which tells you which half of the morning I enjoyed more. It was the half where I was standing still.

What I learned: on an aspen day, don't shoot into the sun-facing side. Put the light behind the leaves and keep something dark behind the tree. The gold does the rest.

episode.title: The ride that kept stopping
episode.script:
Narrated by GlazyArray.

It was a little after ten on a clear October morning at Spooner Lake Trailhead, and the sky was the kind of blue that makes you squint.

The last time this show came up the trail toward Marlette Lake, it was just before the trail closed for repairs. Now it was open again. The ranger at the gate said every trail was open, every day. And it looked like everyone had heard. There were a lot more people than usual, and there were horses on the trail too.

On a shared trail, bikes yield to horses, and Christian always does. On the way back, not far from the start, Christian and Marley were stopped at a stream. He'd just had a granola bar when some riders came up on their horses. Friendly riders, and their horses. Christian looked at the spot he and Marley were in and saw it was the best place for the horses to get to the water. They were ready to go anyway. So they packed up and left it to them. He counted it lucky, getting to meet such beautiful creatures. That's good trail manners. It's also just paying attention.

Christian rode, with Marley running alongside him and the bike. Ha-Leen-Ah walked, with Sofi, a black dog they were dog-sitting. They set out together. But a bike and a walker don't keep the same pace, so they split up, and then found each other again, many times, all along the way. Each of them carried their own snacks. It was an out-and-back trail, not a loop. A little bit together, a little bit apart, and together again.

Within half an hour the trail had turned into a hallway of white trunks and yellow leaves. Marley would trot ahead, stop, look back, and wait. Then trot ahead again. Christian stopped too. He took a picture of her standing in the middle of the road, small and brown against all that gold.

Higher up, the trees opened onto a meadow of sage. Beyond it, a whole hillside of aspens had gone yellow and orange below the ridge, with a few dark firs standing in front like they'd been told to hold still for the photo.

***

And then, just after eleven, the ride became something else.

Christian stopped riding and picked up the camera. He didn't just point it at the brightest tree. He waited for the light to come from behind the leaves, so they glowed, and he found the spots where dark pines stood behind them, so the gold had something to shine against. He turned the frame tall, so a single aspen could fill it from bottom to top. That's the part people don't see in a good photograph. It isn't the tree. It's knowing where to stand.

A few minutes later, the walkers and the riders were together again on the road. Ha-Leen-Ah, smiling wide under her sun hat, and Sofi, who seemed to think the whole forest had been arranged for her.

***

The way back ran through a thick stand of aspens that had turned almost entirely orange, the trail threading between them like a tunnel somebody had lit from the inside.

By the numbers, it was about seven miles, a little over nine hundred feet of climbing, with a high point near seven thousand seven hundred feet. His top speed was about twenty-two miles an hour. But here's the number I like best. He was moving for less than an hour, in a ride that took nearly two.

Some rides are about getting somewhere. This one was about coming back, and then stopping, again and again, until the stopping was the whole point.
